newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-DON'T STAND FOR GERMAN GAMESMANSHIP, REF - FERGUSON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DON'T STAND FOR GERMAN GAMESMANSHIP, REF - FERGUSON.

text.p: Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson has called on officials to stand for no German gamesmanship during Wednesday's European Cup semifinal against Borussia Dortmund.
Germans have a reputation abroad for faking fouls.
Ferguson said on Tuesday that players on the European continent sometimes took dramatic dives when they were tackled and also encouraged referees to hand out yellow cards.

"We hope the referee doesn't fall for the European tendency to go down when they are touched. There is a lot of that," the United manager said. "It is the culture. It is like that in a lot of countries. English people don't like to see that.
"You see a lot of players doing that," Ferguson said, making a hand movement like a referee showing a yellow card. "That is where the referee has to be strong tomorrow."

Andy Moeller, Dortmund's main creative midfield force, was once involved in a much-publicised controversy for taking a theatrical dive in the penalty area during a German league match. Television pictures showed that there had been no contact at all with a defender.
The German soccer federation (DFB) has been forced to launch a tough campaign on players who cheat by "diving". The country's television stations often point out offenders.

"We are going to have to show good discipline and good concentration," said Ferguson, who has extensive experience of European football with Aberdeen and the Scottish national team as well as with United. "But I'm not saying 'don't tackle'."
While Dortmund are struggling with injuries, Ferguson was able to report a fully fit squad for the first leg in the Westfalen stadium.

Discipline will be a key factor for the visitors with a capacity crowd of more than 50,000 guaranteed in the compact ground where the fans are close to the pitch. Unlike many German stadia, Dortmund has a British style of ground with no athletics track around the grass.

United's volatile but brilliant Frenchman Eric Cantona is likely to be man-marked by Dortmund's Scot Paul Lambert, who has gained a reputation in the Bundesliga for being very efficient at cancelling out influential players.
Ferguson said he was looking to the most experienced players in his squad such as Cantona and Danish goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel to play key roles in the intense atmosphere.

"Cantona is a big game player. There is no doubt about that," he said. "There are certain players who have a great deal of responsibility. When you get to a semifinal you hope the big team players can do it."

United's defence looked poor in a shock premier league home defeat by unglamorous Derby at the weekend, and Ferguson knows Dortmund's Swiss-German striking partnership of Stephane Chapuisat and Karlheinz Riedle will punish similar mistakes.
"You can't defend like we did on Saturday in any game of football, far be it the semifinal of the European Cup," he said.
